title: Does On-Policy Distillation Really Distill? From Noisy Teacher to Self-Improvement
data_curation: Training uses only the questions of DAPO-17k for math, with no labels, ground-truth answers, hints, or teacher; for code, Open-R1 Codeforces prompts (best checkpoint chosen on MBPP+ validation). The noise analysis samples one correct and one incorrect Qwen3-1.7B response for each of 500 DAPO-17k questions, verified against ground truth, and defines 'noisy' supervision as a teacher advantage on the \boxed{} answer tokens whose sign disagrees with the verifier. The multi-domain variant (MD-OPSA) randomly mixes an equal number of DAPO-17k math and Codeforces code prompts, with no domain routing.
curriculum: Not a focus of this paper. OPSA is a single on-policy stage applied directly to released models (Qwen3-1.7B/4B and Qwen3.5-9B in non-thinking mode, Olmo3-7B Instruct and Think), selecting the best checkpoint by validation Avg@4 every 20 steps. An appendix shows OPSA can serve as a supervision-free 'cold start' before GRPO on DAPO-17k (Qwen3-4B AIME24 Avg@4 up about 9 points after 40 more GRPO steps), and MD-OPSA mixes math and code in one stage instead of training separate domain teachers.
method: First an analysis of OPD (reverse-KL with the K1 estimator, token advantage A = log pi_t - log pi_s): with Qwen3-4B/30B-A3B/235B-A22B-Instruct teachers the answer-token noise rate rises 30.6% -> 34.7% -> 50.6%, yet training only on noisy, only on clean, or on all trajectories converges similarly. 29.2% of tokens get exactly zero advantage and 51.7% have |A| <= 1e-4, concentrated on high-logp tokens; training on top-logp tokens (even with random advantages) gives no gain, while a fixed advantage of -0.5 on the lowest-20%-logp tokens matches OPD and +0.2 collapses. OPSA (On-Policy Self-Adaptation) then updates only the 20% lowest-logp sampled tokens with entropy-adaptive negative advantage A_i = -1/2 - (H_i - H_min)/(2(H_max - H_min)), i.e. stronger penalty at high-entropy forks. This suppresses tail tokens and spreads mass among head tokens. Setup: slime + Megatron + SGLang on 8xH100, LR 1e-6, rollout/global batch 64, 1 sample per prompt, max response 12000, temperature 1.0.
eval_metrics: In-domain math AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25 (Avg@32 and Pass@32, temperature 0.7, top-k 20, top-p 0.8, 32768 max tokens, non-thinking), out-of-domain MBPP+ and GPQA-Diamond; code training is evaluated on LiveCodeBench v6 and HumanEval+. Qwen3-1.7B AIME24 Avg@32 goes from 13.44 to 48.85 (Pass@32 40.00 -> 80.00); Qwen3-4B AIME24 23.33 -> 62.08; Qwen3.5-9B 76.35 -> 87.81; Olmo3-7B Think 71.88 -> 77.29. On Qwen3-1.7B, 3-benchmark average Avg@32: GRPO 24.79, TTRL 11.81, OPD (4B-Instruct teacher) 22.15, OPSD 23.58, NSR 24.13, OPSA 35.83. Diversity is measured with pairwise 4-gram Jaccard distance; efficiency is training step time (GRPO 186.2 s, OPD 61.2 s, OPSA 46.3 s).
key_results: Without any teacher, reward, or hint, OPSA lifts Qwen3-1.7B AIME24 Avg@32 by 35.41 points (a 263% relative gain), more than doubles Pass@32 on all three math benchmarks, and beats OPD by 16.77 points on AIME24 and the best on-policy baseline by 11.04 average Avg@32. Token-budget-matched controls (appending 'wait') do not close the gap: GRPO 32.81 and OPD 31.67 vs OPSA 48.85.
evolution_note: The paper questions the 2025-2026 on-policy distillation line (GKD, MiniLLM, Thinking Machines' K1-estimator OPD, and hint-based self-distillation OPSD) by showing much of OPD's gain comes from suppressing the student's own low-probability tokens, not from teacher knowledge. It connects to negative-sample reinforcement (NSR) and high-entropy 'fork token' findings in RLVR, and to label-free RL such as TTRL and Intuitor, proposing a teacher-free, reward-free token-level objective; the authors note it is tested only up to 9B and may not expand the exploration frontier of already sharp models.
